findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Saudi Arabia
findings.description:
Kafala system and exclusion of domestic workers from labor law protections

Scheme: Recruitment agencies and employers confiscate migrant workers' passports upon arrival, enforce excessive working hours (often 18+ hours/day), and withhold wages under the guise of 'repayment' for recruitment fees. Workers are unable to change employers or leave the country without employer consent, creating a de facto system of forced labor. Complaints to authorities are dismissed due to the exclusion of domestic workers from the Saudi Labor Law (Royal Decree No. M/51, 2005).
tags: Royal Decree No. M/51 (Saudi Labor Law, 2005) - Article 7 excludes domestic workers
Kafala (sponsorship) system under the Ministry of Interior's Residency Regulations
Anti-Trafficking Law (2009) - rarely enforced for labor exploitation cases
SA

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Qatar
findings.description:
Partial kafala reforms with persistent Wage Protection System (WPS) gaps and recruitment fee loopholes

Scheme: Employers exploit the WPS by paying workers' salaries through the system to create a paper trail of compliance, but then force workers to return a portion of their wages in cash. Recruitment agencies charge exorbitant fees (up to $4,000) to workers in origin countries, trapping them in debt bondage. The 2018 kafala reforms allow workers to change jobs without employer consent after 5 years, but this is circumvented by employers who terminate workers just before the 5-year mark. The Labor Law (Law No. 14 of 2004) still lacks protections for domestic workers.
tags: Law No. 14 of 2004 (Labor Law) - excludes domestic workers
Law No. 21 of 2015 (Regulating the Entry, Exit, and Residency of Expatriates) - kafala reforms
Ministerial Decision No. 21 of 2015 (Wage Protection System)
Law No. 15 of 2017 (Domestic Workers Law) - weak enforcement
QA

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Thailand
findings.description:
Fishing vessel exemptions and border worker registration gaps

Scheme: Fishing vessels operating outside Thai territorial waters (beyond 12 nautical miles) are exempt from the Labor Protection Act (1998) and the Fisheries Act (2015). Traffickers exploit this by registering vessels as 'offshore' to avoid inspections, then subject workers to forced labor, physical abuse, and wage theft. Migrant workers from Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos are often smuggled into Thailand without proper registration, making them vulnerable to exploitation. The Royal Ordinance on Fisheries (2015) requires vessel monitoring, but enforcement is weak for smaller boats.
tags: Labor Protection Act (1998) - exempts fishing vessels beyond 12 nautical miles (Section 4)
Fisheries Act (2015) - weak enforcement for small vessels
Royal Ordinance on Fisheries (2015) - vessel monitoring requirements
Royal Ordinance on Management of Migrant Workers (2017) - registration gaps
TH

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Malaysia
findings.description:
Labor outsourcing companies and sector-specific exemptions

Scheme: Employers in the plantation and electronics manufacturing sectors use labor outsourcing companies to hire migrant workers, avoiding direct responsibility for wages, working conditions, and benefits. The Employment Act (1955) does not adequately regulate outsourcing companies, allowing them to charge workers excessive recruitment fees and deduct wages for housing and transportation. The Immigration Act (2002) ties workers' visas to their outsourcing company, making it difficult for them to change employers. The Electronics Industry Code of Conduct (EICC) is voluntary and rarely enforced.
tags: Employment Act (1955) - lacks regulation of outsourcing companies
Immigration Act (2002) - ties visas to employers
Workers' Minimum Standards of Housing and Amenities Act (2019) - weak enforcement
Electronics Industry Code of Conduct (EICC) - voluntary
MY

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Lebanon
findings.description:
Strict kafala system with no labor law coverage for domestic workers and normalized confiscation of passports

Scheme: Recruitment agencies and employers confiscate migrant domestic workers' passports upon arrival, enforce 24/7 work schedules, and withhold wages. The Lebanese Labor Law (Law No. 536/1996) explicitly excludes domestic workers, leaving them with no legal protections. The kafala system requires workers to obtain employer consent to change jobs or leave the country, trapping them in abusive conditions. Complaints to the Ministry of Labor are dismissed, and workers who flee are often arrested for 'illegal residency.' The Anti-Trafficking Law (2011) is rarely enforced for labor exploitation cases.
tags: Lebanese Labor Law (Law No. 536/1996) - Article 7 excludes domestic workers
Kafala system under the General Security Directorate's Residency Regulations
Anti-Trafficking Law (2011) - weak enforcement
Law No. 164/2011 (Anti-Trafficking Law) - rarely applied to labor cases
LB

findings.title: Cross-jurisdiction pattern: labor_law_gaps
findings.description: Criminals exploit migration corridors by combining the strictest aspects of each jurisdiction's labor laws. For example, recruitment agencies in origin countries (e.g., Nepal, Philippines) charge exorbitant fees to workers, trapping them in debt bondage. These workers are then placed in destination countries (e.g., Saudi Arabia, Lebanon) where the kafala system prevents them from leaving abusive employers. In transit countries (e.g., Thailand, Malaysia), traffickers exploit registration gaps to smuggle workers without documentation, increasing their vulnerability. The lack of harmonized labor protections across jurisdictions allows criminals to shift responsibility and avoid accountability. For instance, a worker trafficked from Myanmar to Thailand to Malaysia may face different legal barriers in each country, making it nearly impossible to seek redress.
tags: cross_jurisdiction
meta_pattern

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Delaware (US)
findings.description:
LLC secrecy laws allowing anonymous ownership combined with pending enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA) and the use of series LLCs to fragment ownership

Scheme: A criminal organization establishes a Delaware LLC with anonymous members, using a registered agent to obscure true ownership. They then create multiple series LLCs under the parent LLC, each holding assets or conducting transactions to fragment and conceal illicit funds. The delay in CTA enforcement allows them to exploit the lack of immediate beneficial ownership reporting. Funds are moved through these entities to layer transactions and evade detection by law enforcement.
tags: Delaware Limited Liability Company Act (6 Del. C. § 18-101 et seq.) - Allows anonymous LLCs
Corporate Transparency Act (31 U.S.C. § 5336) - Pending enforcement as of 2024
Delaware Series LLC provisions (6 Del. C. § 18-215) - Permits creation of series with separate assets/liabilities
US-DE

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Nevada (US)
findings.description:
Lack of state corporate income tax, minimal reporting requirements, and allowance of nominee officers to obscure beneficial ownership

Scheme: A human trafficking ring establishes a Nevada LLC with nominee officers (e.g., a law firm or corporate service provider) listed as the public-facing owners. The true beneficiaries remain hidden while the LLC is used to purchase real estate, vehicles, and other assets with illicit proceeds. The lack of state income tax and minimal reporting requirements reduces scrutiny, and nominee officers shield the traffickers from direct association with the assets.
tags: Nevada Revised Statutes (NRS) Chapter 86 - LLC formation with minimal disclosure
NRS 78.037 - Allows nominee officers for corporations/LLCs
Nevada’s lack of state corporate income tax (NRS 363) - Reduces financial transparency
US-NV

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: United Kingdom
findings.description:
Scottish Limited Partnerships (SLPs) with opaque ownership, gaps in Companies House verification, and trust opacity for concealing beneficial owners

Scheme: A Russian oligarch uses a Scottish Limited Partnership (SLP) to launder money through the UK. The SLP is registered with Companies House, but the partners (often shell companies in offshore jurisdictions) are not verified. The oligarch also uses a UK trust to hold the SLP’s assets, further obscuring ownership. The SLP is then used to move funds through UK banks, exploiting the lack of due diligence on SLPs and the opacity of trusts.
tags: Limited Partnerships Act 1907 - Governs SLPs with minimal transparency
Companies Act 2006 - Gaps in Companies House verification (e.g., no ID checks for partners)
UK Trust Law - Allows opaque beneficial ownership structures
UK

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Netherlands
findings.description:
Extensive tax treaty network, cooperative structures with minimal substance requirements, and conduit arrangements for routing illicit funds

Scheme: A Latin American drug cartel sets up a Dutch cooperative (Coöperatie) to act as a conduit for moving drug proceeds. The cooperative has no real business activity in the Netherlands but exploits the country’s tax treaties to avoid withholding taxes on cross-border transactions. The cartel also uses the cooperative to invest in European real estate and securities, layering the funds through multiple jurisdictions to obscure their origin. The lack of substance requirements for cooperatives makes this scheme difficult to detect.
tags: Dutch Civil Code (Book 2, Title 3) - Governs cooperatives with minimal transparency
Netherlands’ tax treaty network (e.g., treaties with Panama, Luxembourg) - Enables treaty shopping
EU Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD) - Loopholes in substance requirements for cooperatives
NL

findings.title: Cross-jurisdiction pattern: corporate_transparency_gaps
findings.description: Criminals frequently combine jurisdictions to create multi-layered opacity. For example, a Delaware LLC (anonymous ownership) might be used to hold a Nevada LLC (nominee officers), which in turn owns a Scottish LP (opaque partners) that routes funds through a Dutch cooperative (tax treaty benefits). This cross-jurisdictional structuring exploits regulatory gaps in each jurisdiction, such as weak beneficial ownership reporting (US), lack of verification (UK), and tax treaty networks (NL), to create near-impenetrable opacity for illicit funds. The use of trusts (UK) or series LLCs (DE) adds additional layers, making tracing and enforcement extremely difficult.
tags: cross_jurisdiction
meta_pattern

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: DeFi (No Jurisdiction)
findings.description:
Regulatory void - absence of KYC/AML requirements, pseudonymous transactions, and smart contract automation enabling irreversible, cross-border transfers without oversight.

Scheme: Criminals exploit DeFi protocols to launder illicit funds through 'mixing' services (e.g., Tornado Cash) or cross-chain bridges to obfuscate transaction trails. Funds are then converted into privacy coins (e.g., Monero) or fiat via unregulated OTC desks. The lack of jurisdictional oversight allows for seamless integration with other high-risk jurisdictions (e.g., UAE free zones) to cash out.
tags: No direct laws apply due to decentralized nature, but FATF's 'Travel Rule' (Recommendation 16) is circumvented as DeFi protocols do not comply with transaction monitoring requirements.
OFAC sanctions (e.g., Tornado Cash designation in 2022) highlight enforcement challenges but do not eliminate the gap.
GLOBAL

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: El Salvador
findings.description:
Bitcoin as legal tender with minimal regulation - no capital gains tax on Bitcoin, residency-by-investment program, and lack of robust AML/KYC enforcement for crypto transactions.

Scheme: Criminals exploit El Salvador's residency-by-investment program ($1M Bitcoin investment) to gain tax residency while laundering funds. Bitcoin is used to purchase real estate or businesses, which are then sold for clean fiat. The absence of capital gains tax on Bitcoin allows for tax-free profit realization. Additionally, unregulated Bitcoin ATMs and exchanges facilitate cashing out illicit funds without scrutiny.
tags: Bitcoin Law (Decree No. 57, 2021) - establishes Bitcoin as legal tender but lacks AML/KYC provisions for crypto transactions.
Residency-by-Investment Program (Decree No. 69, 2021) - allows residency with $1M Bitcoin investment, no source-of-funds verification.
Tax Code (Article 4) - exempts Bitcoin from capital gains tax.
SV

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: UAE (VASP Hub)
findings.description:
Light-touch VASP licensing in free zones (e.g., DMCC, ADGM) - minimal AML/KYC requirements for licensed entities, privacy-friendly corporate structures, and lack of public beneficial ownership registries.

Scheme: Criminals establish VASPs (e.g., crypto exchanges or OTC desks) in UAE free zones to facilitate large-scale money laundering. Licensed VASPs are used to onboard illicit funds under the guise of compliance, while privacy-friendly free zone entities (e.g., RAK ICC) obscure beneficial ownership. Funds are then integrated into the global financial system via UAE banks or real estate investments.
tags: UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering - requires VASPs to register but lacks stringent enforcement.
DMCC Crypto Regulations (2021) - light-touch licensing for crypto businesses in the free zone.
ADGM's Regulatory Framework for Virtual Assets (2018) - requires VASP licensing but allows for privacy-friendly corporate structures.
AE

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Malta
findings.description:
Early crypto framework with loopholes - VFA (Virtual Financial Assets) Act allows for exchange licensing but lacks strict enforcement, and the MFSA (regulator) has limited capacity to monitor cross-border transactions.

Scheme: Criminals exploit Malta's VFA licensing to operate seemingly compliant exchanges that facilitate money laundering. Licensed exchanges are used to onboard illicit funds, which are then traded for privacy coins or transferred to unregulated jurisdictions (e.g., DeFi protocols). The lack of robust cross-border transaction monitoring allows for seamless integration with other high-risk jurisdictions.
tags: Virtual Financial Assets Act (VFA Act, 2018) - establishes licensing for crypto exchanges but lacks strict AML enforcement.
Malta Financial Services Authority (MFSA) Guidelines - require VASPs to comply with AML/CFT but lack resources for enforcement.
Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA, 1994) - applies to VASPs but is weakly enforced for crypto transactions.
MT

findings.title: Cross-jurisdiction pattern: crypto_regulation_gaps
findings.description: Criminals exploit regulatory asymmetries by combining jurisdictions in a 'layering' process: (1) Onboard illicit funds via DeFi protocols (no KYC), (2) move funds to El Salvador for tax-free conversion to Bitcoin, (3) route through UAE VASPs for 'compliant' onboarding, and (4) integrate into the global financial system via Maltese exchanges or real estate investments. This creates a 'compliance facade' where each jurisdiction's regulatory gaps are exploited sequentially to obfuscate the origin of funds.
tags: cross_jurisdiction
meta_pattern
